title: 38-10_Gr. of Packer
text:
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
GRIEVANCE OF: )
) DOCKET NO. 22-43
JONATHAN PACKER )
FINDINGS OF FACT, OPINION, AND ORDER
Vermont State Employees’ Association (“VSEA”), on behalf of Jonathan Packer, grieves
the State’s actions in refusing to permit him to attend a virtual meeting of the Labor Management
Committee for the Vermont Psychiatric Care Hospital/Middlesex Therapeutic Community
Residence (“VPCH/MTCR”), a time when he was appointed to that committee by the VSEA as
its chair, and while he was on temporary relief from duty. VSEA alleges the State (“Employer”)
violated the CBA by denying its request to select its own representative to the committee.
VSEA has also included an unfair labor practice charge asserting the State violated 3
V.S.A. § 961 (1), when it interfered, restrained, or coerced Mr. Packer and VSEA in the exercise
of their rights guaranteed under 3 V.S.A. § 903.
The parties provided stipulated facts and presented briefing to the Board Panel comprised
of Robert Greemore, Chair, Alan Willard, and David Boulanger.
FINDINGS OF FACT
1. At all times relevant to this grievance, Jonathan Packer, (hereinafter referred to as
“Grievant”), was a permanent status employee of the DMH, as an Associate Mental
Health Specialist.
2. The Respondent Vermont Department of Mental Health is an agency of the State of
Vermont with offices at 280 State Drive, NOB 2 North, Waterbury Vermont 05671.
10

3. At all times relevant to this grievance, the State and the VSEA have been parties to the
Non-Management Unit Collective Bargaining Agreements, ("the Contract"), in effect for
the period from July 1, 2020, to June 30, 2022. As such, the State, VSEA, and the
Grievant are entitled to all rights afforded to the employer, the bargaining agent and
employees by the Contract, the rules and regulations for personnel administration, and by
statute.
4.Article 1 of the NMU Contract provides in pertinent part that:
The State of Vermont recognizes the Vermont State Employees’ Association, Inc. as the
exclusive representative of the Vermont State employees in the Non-Management
Bargaining Unit.
5.Article 2 of the NMU contract provides in pertinent part that:
Subject to law, rules and regulations, including, for example, 3 VSA 311(a)(10) and 3
VSA 327(a), and subject to terms set forth in this Agreement, nothing in this Agreement
shall be construed to interfere with the right of the Employer to carry out the statutory
mandate and goals of the agency, to restrict the State in its reserved and retained lawful
and customary management rights, powers and prerogatives, including the right to utilize
personnel, methods and means in the most appropriate manner possible . . .
6.Article 3 of the NMU Contract provides in pertinent part that:
VSEA TIME OFF: Subject to the efficient conduct of State business, which shall prevail
in any instance of conflict, permission for reasonable time off during normal working
hours without loss of pay and without charge to accrued benefits shall not be
unreasonably withheld.
…
Subject to the foregoing, time off shall be granted in the following instances to:
….
(g)Members of Labor Management Committees for meetings scheduled by the State and
VSEA.
7. Article 7 of the NMU Contract provides in pertinent part:
…
3.The parties agree that Agencies, Departments, facilities, or local worksites may
establish labor-management committees. Upon written request of the VSEA or
11

the State, an Agency or Department must establish a labor-management
committee for a six (6) month period to meet periodically and to discuss a
mutually agreed upon agenda. After it is established it may be extended (or
reinstituted after it lapses) only by mutual written agreement for additional six (6)
month periods at the discretion of the Agency, Department and the VSEA. The
numbers of participants, selected in equal numbers by the appointing authorities
and VSEA, shall depend on the needs of the group and the agenda items to be
discussed and may exceed four (4) persons for labor or management with the
approval of the appointing authority in any instance. These Committees shall meet
as needed to discuss issues of mutual concern; provided, however, these sessions
are not for the purpose of discussing pending grievances or for collective
bargaining on any subject. In the event the parties call a meeting, the Human
Resources Department and the VSEA central office shall be notified at least three
(3)working days prior to the meeting and may participate.
8.Article 14 of the NMU contract provides in pertinent part that:
An appointing authority may relieve employees from duty temporarily with pay
for a period of up to thirty (30) workdays: (a) to permit the appointing authority to
investigate or make inquiries into charges and allegations made by or concerning
the employee; or (b) if in the judgment of the appointing authority the employee’s
continued presence at work during the period of investigation is detrimental to the
best interests of the State, the public, the ability of the office to perform its work
in the most efficient manner possible, or well being or morale of persons under
the State’s care. The period of temporary relief from duty may be extended by the
appointing authority, with the concurrence of the Commissioner of Human
Resources. Employees temporarily relieved from duty shall be notified in writing
within twenty-four (24) hours with specific reasons given as to the nature of the
investigation, charges and allegations. Notices of temporary relief from duty with
pay shall contain a reference to the right of the employee to request representation
by VSEA, or private counsel, in any interrogation connected with the
investigation or resulting hearing
9. At all times relevant herein, the Grievant has been appointed by the VSEA as a union
steward and as a representative and the VSEA chair of the Vermont Psychiatric Care
Hospital/Middlesex Therapeutic Community Residence (“VPCH /MTCR”) Labor
Management Committee.
10. In April and May of 2022, the other VSEA representatives on the Labor Management
Committee were John Berger (Associate Mental Health Specialist at VPCH) and Bridget
Aldridge (Nurse Supervisor at VPCH) and the management members were Stephanie
12

Shaw (Executive Director, Chief Nursing Executive at VPCH), Grace Winters (interim
appointment to Executive Director filling in for Stephanie Shaw at VPCH), Troy Parah
(Secure Residential Program Director at MTCR Facility) , Karen Barber (DMH General
Counsel, Waterbury), Daryl Hall (former VPCH CEO) and Tammie Ellison (DHR
Administrator, Barre).
11. On February 15, 2022, an incident occurred between Grievant and a VPCH patient which
gave rise to allegations of misconduct on the part of the Grievant.
12. On February 16, 2022, the Department sent the Grievant a letter, attached hereto as
Exhibit B, which placed him on temporary relief from duty (TRFD) with pay pending
investigation into the February 15 incident and stated in part as follows:
Do not engage in any work activity related to the Department of Mental Health
(“DMH”) without specific authorization of your supervisor. Unless specifically
approved by your supervisor, do not use any DMH equipment or access any DMH
files, including computer files. Do not visit your work site or other Agency or
DMH work sites, and do not contact DMH employees on work-related matters.
13. When State employees are placed on TRFD with pay pending review of an investigatory
matter involving alleged misconduct, the standard TRFD letter contains an instruction to
the employee being placed on TRFD that they not engage in “any work activity related to
the Department without specific authorization of [their] supervisor.” The State has been
using this language for over two decades. VSEA has been aware of the State’s
longstanding practice of restricting employees on TRFD from performing their job duties
on behalf of the employer, but VSEA has never waived its right to designate such
employees as its representatives and agents in its role as exclusive bargaining agent.
14. DHR Investigator Jim Morris was assigned to investigate the allegations against the
grievant and conducted the following interviews:
13

Person Interviewed, Witness/Subject Date of Interview(s)
Position
Michelle Uline Mental Witness March 11, 2022
health specialist
Renee Spaulding Mental Witness March 22, 2022
health specialist
Jessica Benway Witness March 21, 2022
Mental health specialist
Roger Hill Charge nurse Witness March 22, 2022
Samantha Lepage Witness March 22, 2022
Registered nurse
Jonathan Packer Mental Subject March 31, 2022
health specialist
15. On April 6, 2022, Investigator Morris forwarded an investigative report to DMH
Commissioner Emily Hawes and DHR General Counsel Thomas Waldman. In its last
paragraph, the report states that the Grievant was asked about the interaction with
Winters and Shaw when they placed him on leave, and that he admitted that he had been
sarcastic, and that he believed the employer’s actions were ridiculous and responded
accordingly. On April 15, 2022, HR Administrator Tammie Ellison scheduled a staffing
meeting on April 20 for the DMH Management team to meet with DHR Legal and DHR
Labor Relations staff to discuss the Packer investigation.
16. At some point in early April 2022, the VSEA and the Department scheduled a Labor
Management Committee meeting to be held on April 20.
17. On April 19, VSEA Field Representative Rachael Fields sent Human Resources
Administrator Tammie Ellison the message dated 4/19 at 1:27 p.m. which stated as
follows:
We have a LMC scheduled for tomorrow. Jo Packer will be attending virtually. I
have seen nothing in his investigation which warrants him not being present
virtually as a VSEA representative.
14

I have received the following agenda items:
1. MTCR staff feel left out when management sends email communications
which only mention VPCH.
2. A lot of the recruitment and retention issues may be related to hiring practices
and not supporting promotion within.
3. Training have become insufficient in that they haven’t been in person or via
Teams in years and often times are only emails. Please let me know if you
have more to add.
18. Ms. Ellison responded as follows on April 20 at 10:01 a.m.
After speaking with Labor Relations, the State contends that Jo’s participation as
a VSEA Steward at the VPCH LMC meeting today would be in violation of the
temporary relief of duty letter as the LMC is directly tied to his employment at
VPCH/DMH. Whereas if Jo was requesting to take leave to be able to attend a
counsel [sic] meeting, an executive meeting, training, etc. that would ne nor [sic]
a violation.
19. On May 4, 2022, a second staffing meeting was held between the DMH management
team, DHR Legal, and DHR Labor Relations to continue their inquiry into the allegations
against Mr. Packer.
20. On June 3, 2022, VPCH CEO Daryl Hall met with the grievant and discussed the
conditions under which he would return to work at the VPCH. Grievant was issued a
written reprimand, [Exhibit E]. CEO Hall advised grievant of two additional
expectations. First, Grievant was expected to successfully complete Pro-ACT training on
June 8, June 9, and June 10, 2023 and complete a written report detailing his
understanding of appropriate and acceptable de-escalation techniques to Grace Winters,
Interim Chief Nursing Executive. Grievant was also expected to complete four (4)
individual sessions with Dr. Greg Tomasulo, Director of Psychology, focusing on
awareness, non-verbal intimidation, and appropriate de-escalation techniques. Grievant’s
TRFD with pay status ended on June 8, 2022 and he returned to his regular duties after
15

completing the three days of Pro-ACT training. The VSEA has grieved the written
reprimand and the grievance remains pending at this time.
21. On August 1, 2022, the VSEA timely filed the instant Step IV grievance at the Labor
Board raising the challenges set forth in this grievance.
OPINION
The Union asserts the Employer violated the Contract, and the State Employees Labor
Relations Act (“SELRA”), 3 V.S.A. § 903, when Employer prohibited Grievant, its chosen chair,
access to and participation in a Labor Management Committee (“LMC”) meeting with
Employer. Although the VSEA has filed both a Grievance and unfair labor practice charge, the
Board must first review the Grievance to determine whether it is arbitrable or subject to the
dispute resolution process in the Contract. If it is, the Board must defer to that grievance
procedure. Parties to a collective bargaining agreement must first exhaust all contractual
remedies before an unfair labor practice charge will lie. See, e.g., Burlington Area Pub. Emps.
Union, Loc. 1343, AFSCME, AFL-CIO v. Champlain Water Dist., 156 Vt. 516, 518 (1991).
Grievant has alleged the Employer violated Articles I, III, and VII of the Contract. The
Contract provides a grievance process to redress noncompliance with the Contract. The Board
will defer to this process agreed to by the parties to resolve the present dispute.
The parties agree that Grievant was selected and appointed by the VSEA as a union
steward and as a representative and VSEA Chair of the Vermont Psychiatric Care
Hospital/Middlesex Therapeutic Community Residence (“VPCH/MTCR”) Labor Management
Committee. The Contract provides the Union with the right to appoint its representatives to
labor-management committees. Article 7.
16

The Employer asserts its actions did not prohibit Grievant from obtaining leave time for
VSEA activities, but “only restricted Grievant from entering the workplace and interacting with
patients and state employees.” Article 14 of the Contract authorizes the Employer to place
employees on leave pending the outcome of disciplinary investigations. Grievant was on
temporary relief from duty (“TRFD”) and instructed not to “engage in any work activity related
to the Department of Mental Health (“DMH”) without specific authorization of your supervisor.”
The TRFD letter contained language Employer has used for decades advising Grievant not to
engage in “any work activity related to the Department.” Grievant’s role at the Labor
Management Committee, Employer claims, qualifies as “work activity related to the Department
of Mental Health,” and therefore, it properly prevented Grievant from attending the LMC
meeting. The Employer contends enforcing the mandatory leave by preventing Grievant’s
attendance was consistent with its TRFD letter.
The LMC meeting was scheduled as a virtual meeting. Grievant would not be attending
in person. The subjects of the meeting were not related to Grievant’s conduct or his work duties,
but rather general issues of recruitment and retention, training, and communication. Grievant’s
role in attending the LMC meeting was to represent Union members and the interests of the
Union. Grievant’s attendance and participation at the Labor Relations Committee meeting was
not in performance of his job duties, nor on behalf of his employer.
The Employer claims that Article 3, Section 3, supports its decision to deny the request
for Grievant to attend the LMC meeting, The Contract provides “subject to the efficient conduct
of State business, which shall prevail in any instance of conflict,” requests by members of the
LMC for “reasonable time off during normal working hours without loss of pay and without
charge to accrued benefits shall not be unreasonably withheld.” Article 3. Because Grievant was
17

on leave and under investigation for alleged unprofessional behavior towards patients and his
supervisors, the Employer contends it properly denied approval for attendance at the LMC
meeting to avoid disruption of the work site and to promote the efficient conduct of State
business.
The LMC meeting was to be held remotely by ZOOM, not at the psychiatric hospital, and
none of the witnesses interviewed regarding Grievant’s alleged misconduct were to participate at
the LMC meeting. Compare Findings 10 with 14. The issues to be discussed did not relate to
Grievant’s job duties nor the subject of his Grievance. Grievant would also not be discussing or
using the meeting to litigate his grievance. Indeed, the Contract prohibits LMC meetings to be
used “for the purpose of discussing pending grievances or collective bargaining on any subject.”
Article 7, § 3. Grievant was not returning to his work site and would not be interfering with the
efficient conduct of State business to attend the virtual meeting.
The Employer relies on the response of Ms. Ellison to justify its denying Grievant his
right to attend the LCM conference. Ms. Ellison explains that although Grievant could attend a
council meeting, training, or executive meeting, he could not attend the LMC meeting without
violating the TRFD. The Employer has not sufficiently distinguished the duties of an employee
acting as a union representative at a council or executive meeting from that of an employee
acting as a union representative at an LMC meeting. The employee dons their union hat and acts
as a union representative when acting and participating in each of these functions. If attendance
at a council or executive meeting does not violate the TRFD letter, the Board is not convinced
that attendance at the LMC does.
The Employer has not presented any evidence that past practice supports its
interpretation that employees on TRFD are prohibited from participating in Union activities or
18

that Grievant’s alleged misconduct which precipitated the investigation and TRFD warranted
prohibiting Grievant from attending the meeting. The State’s history of using the TRFD letter
restricting employees from performing work related functions does not establish or demonstrate
its authority to prohibit those employees from acting as Union representatives nor deny such
representatives the ability to participate in LMC meetings.
The Employer denied the Union its right to have its chosen representative attend the
Labor Management Committee meeting, contrary to the clear requirements of the Contract.
19

ORDER
The Grievance of the VSEA is Sustained and the Employer must cease and desist from
restraining or interfering with the VSEA’s right to select its representatives for the Labor
Management Committee.
Dated this 23rd day of April 2025, at Montpelier, Vermont.
